zh_summary: 回覆 @TSPsmart 和 @LanceRoberts：說「只要把稅提高到FDR水平」是錯誤敘事。自1945年以來，無論最高邊際稅率如何，美國從未徵收超過GDP的20%。此外，FDR時代有資本管制，這意味著結束1971年後的美元儲備地位。沒有提及個股。

name: The Kobeissi Letter
zh_summary: 美國赤字儘管低失業率仍在飆升。自2020年以來累計美國財政赤字飆升至14.18萬億美元。同時7年平均失業率下降0.4個百分點至4.7%。僅FY2026前11個月赤字總計1.97萬億美元，為該時期歷史第三大。當經濟強、失業率低時，政府通常會保持較低財政赤字，為經濟疲軟保留大規模財政支持。這次卻在失業率穩定下赤字處於歷史高位。這因政府支出高和利息成本上升，即使無衰退赤字仍異常大。大規模赤字已成為美國經濟的永久特徵。沒有提及個股。

FY2026 첫 11개월만의 적자가 1.97조 달러로 이 기간 역사상 세 번째로 큽니다. 경제가 강하고 실업률이 낮을 때 정부는 일반적으로 재정 적자를 낮게 유지하고 경제 약세 기간을 위해 대규모 재정 지원을 예약합니다. 이번에는 안정된 실업률에도 적자가 역사적 고수준입니다. 높은 정부 지출과 상승하는 이자 비용으로 경기 침체 없이도 적자가 예외적으로 큽니다. 대규모 적자는 미국 경제의 영구적 특징이 되었습니다. 개별 종목에 대한 언급이 없습니다.
text:
The US deficit is surging despite low unemployment.

The cumulative US fiscal deficit since 2020 has surged to a massive $14.18 trillion.

Meanwhile, the 7-year average unemployment rate has fallen -0.4 percentage points, to 4.7% over the same period.

In the first 11 months of FY2026 alone, the US deficit totaled $1.97 trillion, the 3rd-largest for this period of the year in history.

When the economy is strong and unemployment is low, the government would typically keep fiscal deficits lower, reserving large-scale fiscal support for periods of economic weakness.

This time, however, the deficit is running at historically high levels despite stable unemployment.

This comes as elevated government spending and rising interest costs are keeping the deficit exceptionally large even without a recession.

Massive deficits have become a permanent feature of the US economy.

zh_summary: 關於「2009年和2020年的600-1000個基點赤字跳躍主要來自酌情刺激（ARRA，CARES）」。這在2001年衰退和1991年衰退中也是如此 - 赤字從峰到谷上升600個基點的GDP。而2009年和尤其2020年「酌情刺激」的原因是防止系統崩潰（和美債市場），因為他們需要把增長推回高於利率，否則面臨債務死亡螺旋，否則美債市場會崩潰。Druckenmiller在2021年CNBC上給了關於這個的採訪。沒有提及個股。
ko_summary: '2009년과 2020년의 600-1000bp 적자 점프는 대부분 재량 자극(ARRA, CARES)에서 왔다'에 대해. 이것은 2001년 경기 침체와 1991년 경기 침체에서도 사실이었으며 적자가 피크에서 트로프까지 GDP의 600bp 상승했습니다. 2009년과 특히 2020년 '재량 자극'의 이유는 시스템 붕괴(및 UST 시장)를 방지하기 위해서였습니다. 성장을 금리 이상으로 밀어 올려야 했기 때문이며 그렇지 않으면 부채 죽음 나선을 직면하거나 UST 시장이 붕괴했을 것입니다. Druckenmiller가 2021년 CNBC에서 이에 대한 인터뷰를 했습니다. 개별 종목에 대한 언급이 없습니다.
text:
RE: "The 600-1,000 bps deficit jumps in 2009 and 2020 came mostly from discretionary stimulus (ARRA, CARES)."

This was also true in the 2001 recession & the 1991 recession - deficit rose 600 bps of GDP, peak to trough.

And the reason for the "discretionary stimulus" in 2009 & esp. 2020 was to prevent systemic collapse of the system (& UST markets), because they needed to push growth back above rates or face a debt death spiral, or the UST market would have collapsed.  

Druckenmiller gave an interview about this on CNBC in 2021 👇

text:
AI token prices have fallen more than 50% since May to under $1 per million tokens but a lot of that reflects usage shifting toward cheaper models rather than broad price cuts.

Open models now account for ~60% of top model traffic at just $0.83 per million tokens while paid models average $6.03 as $GOOGL, OpenAI and Anthropic compete at the high end.

The AI economy is going to continue splitting between cheap intelligence driving massive usage and premium models retaining pricing power which is why falling average token costs don't necessarily mean weaker compute demand for $NVDA, $AVGO and $AMD.

ko_summary: 저자는 $OSS가 자신의 피지컬 AI 바스켓에서 가장 작은 회사 중 하나이며 계속 담고 있다고 했다. 드론, 군용 차량, 자율 시스템이 센서 데이터를 현장에서 처리할 때 필요한 러기드 컴퓨팅을 만들며, 일반 데이터센터 하드웨어가 들어가지 못하는 자리를 메운다고 한다. 군 플랫폼에 설계되면 교체가 어려워 매출이 붙을 수 있다고 본다.
text:
$OSS is one of the smallest companies in my 'Physical AI' basket and I’ve been adding because it builds rugged AI computing systems for defense platforms where traditional data center hardware cannot operate.

As drones, military vehicles and autonomous systems process more sensor data locally that's where OSS comes in by providing the high-performance compute needed for real time AI without relying on cloud.

What I also like is once OSS hardware gets designed into a military platform then replacing it becomes much harder creating a potentially sticky revenue opportunity as defense spending shifts toward autonomy across air, land and sea.

text:
Shocking stat of the day:

$241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds.

This figure is up +1,621% from just $14 billion at the start of 2026.

This means ~38% of French high-grade corporate debt is now trading at lower yields than government bonds of similar maturity.

The gap between corporate and government bond yields is widening as investor concerns about France's deteriorating fiscal situation weigh on government debt.

As a result, internationally exposed companies such as L'Oreal, $OR, and TotalEnergies, $TTE, are increasingly viewed as safer alternatives to French government debt, unlike French banks, which remain more exposed to sovereign risk.

This is in stark contrast to normal economic conditions, when government bonds are traditionally viewed as the safest part of the bond market.

France's corporate bond market is increasingly being treated a safer bet than its government bonds.

ticker_notes.TSLA: 自動駕駛將商品化須靠執行

zh_summary: 作者認為 $TSLA 多頭仍未明白，3 至 5 年內各網約車服務都會一併提供有司機與自動駕駛選項，無人監督的自動駕駛會像汽車業以往的創新一樣變成商品。他說自己並非不看重 FSD，而是認為特斯拉必須靠廣告與執行吃到先發優勢，否則可能像過去 5 年電動車那樣被中國與其他廠商搶走生意。
ko_summary: 저자는 $TSLA 강세론이 3년에서 5년 안에 모든 차량호출 서비스가 기사 운전과 자율주행을 함께 제공하고, 무감독 자율주행이 과거 자동차 혁신처럼 범용재가 된다는 점을 아직 모른다고 했다. FSD를 무시하는 것은 아니며, 테슬라가 광고와 실행으로 선발 우위를 확보하지 못하면 지난 5년 전기차처럼 중국과 다른 제조사에 사업을 뺏길 수 있다고 본다.
text: $TSLA bulls still don’t get that within 3-5 years, every ride hailing service will offer both chauffeured and self-driving options for all their products (Uber Black, Uber X, Uber XL). It’s not that I don’t value FSD, it’s just that unsupervised autonomy will become a commodity just as every other innovation in the history of the automotive industry has become commoditized (and I don’t buy that this time will be different).  Given that, it’s critical that $TSLA figure out how to exploit its first mover advantage through superior advertising and execution rather than let the Chinese and other manufacturers take their business as happened in EVs the past 5 years.

text:
Species and companies get wiped out by technological change all the time, crypto is no different.

While I agree that, at the macro level, if Bitcoin is susceptible then so is conventional banking, at the micro-level it's totally different.

If my bank gets hacked by AI, I will be reimbursed.

If my wallet gets hacked by AI, I have just lost all the money I had on it.

Traditional banking can iterate through problems like this much more easily than crypto can, so even if you are right that it will ultimately survive, have fun living through that.

That's why I sold. I don't want to deal with it. There are better things to focus on than whether or not the latest AI-driven crypto development requires me to sepd the next 48 hours furiously replacing all my cold crypto wallets.

Sacks는 하루만 늦었어도 PayPal은 없었을 것이라며 버블을 알아본 사람은 Thiel뿐이라고 했다. 마지막 문장은 끝나지 않았다. $PYPL을 언급했지만 현재 주가에 대한 입장은 없다.
text:
.@DavidSacks on the time Peter Thiel saved PayPal:

“I really liked working with him. When he hired me, he basically told me, ‘I need people here who I can scream at.’”

“I think what he meant by that was, I need people who can scream at me too. People who will be honest, and you don't even have to worry about hurting people's feelings.”

“He's a great contrarian thinker. I think that was the unique thing he brought—he'd always come up with these strategic insights that everybody else had just kind of missed.”

“Right before the dot-com crash in early 2000, Peter was raising a financing round for us and we got something like $200M in commitments to invest at a $500 million pre-money valuation. PayPal had no revenue, no profits, and not even really a business model.”

“This is the peak of the dot-com euphoria. Everyone in the company was saying, ‘That's too cheap, this is a bad deal, we can't do this.’”

“He's like, ‘Take it.’”

“We got the deal done the Friday before Black Monday. If we had waited just one more day—game over. There would not have been a PayPal.”

“He was the only one who really saw the bubble for what it was.”

“If it wasn't for his contrarian thinking, we would have been swept away with the rest of the bubble companies.”

Via @Jason 2010

Themes of the Week
The long end ripped to levels last seen before the Global Financial Crisis and the S&P still printed a record, because with the Bond Floor gone the only thing holding the longest-duration names over the canyon is Growth, while a soft jobs print kept Goldilocks on its feet, Oil stayed two-sided, and China pressed on every front at once.

Anyone who grew up on Saturday-morning cartoons knows the moment: Wile E. Coyote sprints off the edge of the mesa, legs still churning, and stays aloft right up until the instant he looks down. The backup in long rates has quietly pulled the implicit Bond Floor out from under valuations, and the only thing keeping the Mag-7 complex suspended over the canyon is the Growth story.

zh_summary: 回覆自己的討論，稱 Sirius（SIRI）用戶忠誠，月流失率約 1.5%，對比 Netflix（NFLX）為 2.0% 至 2.5%，Prime Video 約 3.5%，串流業平均為 5% 至 6%。疫情把需求提前，其後增長停滯，現在這段時期結束。儘管加價，用戶基數仍溫和增長並保持穩定。2025 年流失 35 萬用戶，第二季已回到增長，新增 2.2 萬，裝機用戶約 3300 萬。
ko_summary: 자신의 글에 이어서, Sirius(SIRI) 가입자는 충성도가 높고 월 이탈률이 약 1.5%라고 했다. Netflix(NFLX)는 2.0%에서 2.5%, Prime Video는 약 3.5%, 스트리밍 업계 평균은 5%에서 6%라고 비교했다. 팬데믹이 수요를 앞당긴 뒤 가입자 증가가 멈췄지만 이제 그 구간이 끝난다고 했다. 가격을 올려도 가입자 기반은 소폭 늘며 안정적이다. 2025년에 35만 명이 줄었으나 2분기에 2만 2천 명이 늘어 성장으로 돌아왔고, 설치 기반은 약 3300만 명이다.
text: Sirius enjoys a loyal subscriber base with monthly churn around 1.5%. Netflix has monthly churn of 2.0-2.5%, Prime Video’s churn is ~3.5% and the industry average for streaming services is 5-6%. COVID pulled demand forward, causing subscriber growth to stagnate afterward. That’s now ending. The subscriber base has grown modestly and remains stable, even in light of price hikes. Sirius lost 350,000 subscribers in 2025 but has returned to growth, adding 22,000 subscribers in the second quarter. The business has a massive installed base of ~33 million subscribers.

The cost of consumer credit is rising.

The average interest rate on a US credit card rose +0.2 percentage points in August, to 22.36%, its highest level in 12 months.

This is now only 1.0 percentage point below the record 23.37% set in August 2024.

Since 2021, the average credit card interest rate has surged +6.5 percentage points.

By comparison, the 5-year average before the 2020 pandemic was 14.94%.

Meanwhile, the average interest rate on a 5-year new car loan rose +0.4 percentage points in August, to 7.54%, its highest since August 2025.

This is 3.5 percentage points above pre-pandemic levels, but 0.9 percentage points below its all-time high of 8.4%, recorded in August 2024.

Consumer borrowing has rarely been this expensive.

text:
After a wondrous first half for investors, especially for those in growth stocks, the second half of 2026 has been a struggle.  The Russell 3,000 -- which represents roughly 98% of publicly traded US stock market cap -- is up about 3% in the 2nd half, but the average stock in the index is actually down 4.4%.

Along with rising interest rates hurting the most interest-rate sensitive areas of the market, it appears as if the shorts are betting big and winning these days.

We broke the Russell 3,000 into deciles (10 groups of roughly 300 stocks each) based on each stock's short interest as a percentage of its equity float.  We then calculated the average 2nd half percentage change of the stocks in each decile.

Decile one in the chart below all the way to the left of the image, contains the decile of most heavily shorted stocks in the Russell 3,000.  Stocks in this decile are down an average of 13.6% in the 2nd half.  As short interest levels get smaller, performance gets better, and the two deciles containing the least heavily shorted stocks are actually averaging gains in the 2nd half.

During big market rallies, shorts feel the pain and usually push prices higher as they rush to cover.  We're definitely not in that type of environment now, and we haven't been for months.

text:
Contrary to what many on X believe, I am not a $TSLA hater.  From 2019-2023, $TSLA was my largest position.  In investing, valuation vs price has to matter and if you’re not regularly calculating the difference, you’re not a serious investor. My issue with $TSLA now is that price seems high relative to my estimate of value, so I either wait for future earnings and cash flows to move higher (they are declining right now - see below), or for the stock price to move lower to become attractive again.  

$TSLA stock has significantly underperformed NDX over the past 1, 3, and 5 years, as 2026-2030 earnings estimates have declined, as automation has become a commodity, and as valuation became stretched.  So no, I’m not a TSLA hater;  I just don’t care for the current price relative to my estimate of value.

text:
AI will become one of the largest spending categories in the US economy:

AI services are projected to account for a record 8.8% of US GDP in 2032.

This estimate shows how much businesses and consumers are expected to spend per year on the services of AI companies.

This also implies AI companies would generate ~$3.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2032.

By comparison, US consumer spending on food accounts for a similar 9.1% of GDP.

This figure would also be ~72% higher than energy, at 5.1% of GDP, and twice the size of construction as well as computers and software, both at 4.4%.

It would also be nearly 3x defense, at 2.8%, and more than 7x communications and internet, at 1.2% of GDP.

The only category where spending is significantly larger is health, at 18% of GDP.

The scale of the AI revolution is unlike anything seen before.

text:
During the inflationary pressures of 2022, we created our "MORTGAS" consumer misery index that is simply a sum of the price of gas ($/gallon) and the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate.

Our MORTGAS index hit a record low in the early 2020s when mortgage rates got below 3% and prices at the pump briefly got below $2/gallon.  Those days are long gone.

Gas prices first spiked in early 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, then they trended lower for the next few years until they spiked again this year with the US invasion of Iran.

Mortgage rates went from 3% up to 7% during the Fed's massive tightening cycle to address runaway inflation in 2022.  They too had been trending lower over the past few years, but they've moved higher again this year since the Iran War began.

Combined, our MORTGAS index is actually at a new record high right now, eclipsing the peak seen back in October 2023.  Consumers are feeling the pain as we head into midterm elections less than a month away.
